The Adaptive Convexity Framework

Part 1 of 6 · ≈ 22 min read · In pictures · 8 exhibits →

Foundation & Philosophy

By Dale Edward · Corrections and challenges: open an issue on GitHub

Manifesto

The traditional playbook was built for a regime that has ended.

Key takeaways

  • A 60/40 mix of US stocks and 10-year Treasuries earned its reputation as rates fell: about 7.8 percent a year after inflation from 1982 to 2021, against about 3.3 percent from 1946 to 1974, while the last large federal debt was worked down.
  • Federal debt held by the public was 98 percent of GDP in fiscal 2025, and interest was back at its 1991 peak of 3.2 percent of GDP. The 1946 record of 106 percent was never paid off: growth, budget surpluses, capped interest rates and inflation worked it down, and bondholders lost about 1 percent a year after inflation.
  • When inflation, rather than growth, drives uncertainty, stocks and bonds tend to move together. After inflation, 2022 was one of the three worst years since 1928 for a 60/40 mix of US stocks and 10-year Treasuries.
  • Bitcoin is the backbone, held for a supply its protocol caps at 21 million coins. Each of its completed cycles through 2022 fell at least 77 percent from peak to trough, so it is sized to survive a fall of 75 percent or more without a forced sale.
  • Our objective is survivable compounding: survive being wrong, keep exposure to convex payoffs, hold each position in the account that suits how it will be held, sold or passed on, and let written rules act before emotion does.
  • We publish four tests that would prove this thesis wrong, and we will report against them every year.

For four decades a simple portfolio worked. Ten-year Treasury yields fell from above 15 percent in September 1981 to 0.62 percent in July 2020, so bonds paid income and gained in price at the same time. Inflation stayed contained, and from about 2000 bonds also tended to rise when stocks fell. A 60/40 mix of US stocks and 10-year Treasuries returned about 7.8 percent a year after inflation from 1982 to 2021. Much of that reputation was earned by falling rates.

The 2020s run on different terms. Inflation has returned as a separate source of uncertainty: in 2026 the annual rise in consumer prices went from 2.4 percent in January to above 4 percent in May, and was 3.4 percent in August. Central banks now face a conflict they had not faced in forty years. A year after the Federal Reserve began raising rates from near zero, losses on bank bond portfolios helped set off the run that closed Silicon Valley Bank on March 10, 2023. Two days later the Fed announced a facility lending to banks against Treasuries, agency debt and mortgage-backed securities valued at par rather than at market. It kept raising rates that spring, but only behind a new backstop. Fighting inflation and protecting the financial system can now pull in opposite directions.

The post–Cold War order is splitting into competing blocs, and supply chains, reserves and payment systems are splitting with it. Technology pushes the prices of many goods down while asset prices climb, so the consumer price index and the cost of owning assets drift apart. Markets also show : calm and storm arrive in runs.

Judged against consumer prices alone, a portfolio can keep pace with inflation and still fall behind the assets that store wealth. Consumer prices rose about 88 percent from the end of 1999 to the end of 2024. Home prices more than tripled. An equal mix of stocks (with dividends), homes, and gold rose about sixfold.

Not all of that gap is monetary: real growth and falling interest rates account for part of it. Falling rates also hid the cost of debt. From 1991 to 2021, federal debt held by the public rose from about 44 to 94 percent of GDP while the interest bill fell from 3.2 to 1.5 percent of GDP. Then rates rose. By fiscal 2025 the debt stood at 98 percent of GDP on the OMB series plotted below, and the bill was back at about 3.2 percent, level with its 1991 peak, on more than twice the debt.

The arithmetic now runs in a loop. Deficits require new borrowing, new borrowing at higher rates raises the interest bill, and the interest bill widens the deficit. Under current law, the Congressional Budget Office projects that debt held by the public will pass its 1946 record of 106 percent of GDP around 2030 and reach 120 percent by 2036, with net interest rising to 4.6 percent of GDP (February 2026 baseline). When a government’s debt and the cost of carrying it begin to limit what its central bank can do, economists call the condition ; Thomas Sargent and Neil Wallace set out its arithmetic in 1981. We treat it as a governing constraint of this regime, though it has not clearly bound yet. From August 2023 to November 2025 the Federal Reserve held its policy rate at least a point above core inflation while the interest bill climbed past 3 percent of GDP. It then cut three times between September and December 2025, held through the summer of 2026 while core inflation rose back to about 3 percent, and on September 16, 2026 raised its rate for the first time since 2023. A central bank raising rates on top of a 3 percent interest bill is a point against our reading; the first test at the end of this Part says what would show that the constraint is not binding.

The United States has carried a debt this size once before, and how it came down is the most useful precedent we have. Debt held by the public peaked at 106 percent of GDP in 1946 and fell below a quarter of GDP by 1974, although in dollars it was larger in 1974 than in 1946. It was never paid off. From 1942 to 1951 the Federal Reserve held Treasury yields down at the Treasury’s request, with an implicit cap of 2.5 percent on long-term bonds, while consumer prices rose by more than a third between the end of 1945 and the end of 1950. Carmen Reinhart and M. Belen Sbrancia (NBER, 2011) call the result the liquidation of government debt: across the advanced economies they studied, real interest rates were negative roughly half the time between 1945 and 1980, and for the United States and the United Kingdom they estimate the liquidation averaged 3 to 4 percent of GDP a year. Growth alone would not have done it. Julien Acalin and Laurence Ball (NBER, 2023) attribute 51 of the 83 points of decline to primary budget surpluses and distorted interest rates together; without them, the ratio would have fallen only to about 74 percent of GDP. Bondholders carried much of the cost: in Damodaran’s series, 10-year Treasuries lost about 1 percent a year after inflation from 1946 to 1974, while a 60/40 mix still returned about 3.3 percent, carried by its stocks. This time the budget has no surplus to share the work: the CBO baseline has a primary deficit in every year through 2036, 2.6 percent of GDP in 2026 and 2.1 percent in 2036. A portfolio that relies on government bonds for its real return is betting that this debt will be resolved more kindly to bondholders than the last one was.

Volatility and fragility are different risks, and a single volatility figure measures only the first. A portfolio that drops 15 percent in a routine correction and recovers is volatile but sound. A portfolio that takes a permanent loss because its diversifiers fall at the same moment, in a , is . An average volatility figure cannot tell the two apart.

The hedge most portfolios rely on belonged to one period. Through the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, US stocks and Treasuries usually moved together. From about 2000 to 2021 they tended to move in opposite directions, so bonds cushioned equity losses. In 2021 and 2022 the correlation turned positive again. Research at AQR (2023) offers an explanation: stocks and bonds respond in opposite directions to news about growth and in the same direction to news about inflation, so the sign of their correlation depends on which kind of uncertainty dominates. Their model explains about 70 percent of the long-term variation in the US correlation.

In 2022 a 60/40 mix of US stocks and bonds fell about 16 percent: stocks lost about 18 percent with dividends, and bonds, the part meant to cushion them, lost about 13 percent. With 10-year Treasuries as the bond half it was worse: in Damodaran’s series the Treasuries lost 17.8 percent, and 2022 is the only year since 1928 in which US stocks and 10-year Treasuries both fell by more than 10 percent. After inflation the mix lost about 23 percent, a loss matched or exceeded only in 1937 and 1974. In 2022 bondholders lost because yields rose; in the 1940s they lost because yields were held down. The second mechanism is the one this thesis expects. For a retiree drawing 4 percent a year, a loss of that size early in retirement does lasting damage, because withdrawals taken from a smaller balance leave less capital to recover with. That is .

The same years tested a very different holding. Bitcoin fell more than 70 percent twice, in 2018 and again in 2021 and 2022; the second fall, from its November 2021 high to its November 2022 low, was about 77 percent, and in calendar 2022, with inflation at a forty-year high, it lost about 64 percent. Over short spans it has traded like the riskiest of risk assets. A fixed purchase every month from January 2018 to December 2024, made through both falls, still ended at about seven times the money put in. That result requires a position small enough that nothing forces a sale at the bottom, and it says nothing about the next seven years.

Hindsight makes these results look obvious, and they do not show that regime calls can be made reliably in advance. No one knows the timing of a regime change, including us. The framework therefore spends as much effort on surviving a wrong call as on making a right one, and it starts from a different premise:

The objective of portfolio management is not prediction. It is survivable compounding under uncertainty.

A forecast names an outcome and a date. A wrong forecast is expensive, and one that gets the direction right can still miss on timing, which decides whether a position survives long enough for its thesis to be proved.

Timing matters most once withdrawals begin, because they make the order of returns count. Take $1 million, twelve years of returns and $40,000 withdrawn at the end of every year, and run it twice: once with the gains first, once with the same returns in reverse.

is our name for the objective: a portfolio that can be wrong about timing, size or specific outcomes and remain intact, while keeping enough exposure to payoffs, where being right pays far more than being wrong costs. With payoffs of that shape, bought at a sensible price, being right only some of the time can compound to far more than a risk-free return.

That shape has a cost. Near the middle, the curved line sits a little below a plain straight-line bet; that gap is the price of convexity. Sizing keeps the left side survivable, and the right side is left open, within the concentration limits.

We built the framework to be audited: every decision should trace to a written rule or a recorded judgment that the investor could explain to an advisor, a client or an heir. It has seven components, each aimed at a known way traditional portfolios fail:

  1. A macro thesis

    formed and tested by the practitioner, that frames the regime and informs structure. Without one, a portfolio is allocated as if the regime did not matter.

  2. A Bitcoin backbone

    sized to horizon and risk capacity and paced by valuation discipline, with the as one of its lenses. A portfolio that holds none gives up the convexity; one that holds too much without rules invites ruin.

  3. Tax wrappers

    treated as compounding engines, because careless account placement can cost a large share of terminal wealth.

  4. Portfolio construction

    expressed through each position’s (, , ), which classifies a holding by how it behaves in the regime.

  5. Convexity

    governed by scoring, so attachment and sunk cost cannot keep a deteriorating position in the book.

  6. Momentum

    as a trend filter and a governor on drawdowns, so the portfolio neither fights the prevailing trend nor rides a position through a catastrophic fall.

  7. Predefined tripwires and AI-assisted verification

    as the control system for a practitioner with scarce attention and too much information.

The framework holds Bitcoin for what it does. It is a long-duration monetary asset that runs parallel to the dollar system, with a supply capped at 21 million coins by its protocol and growing institutional access. In a regime whose central risk is the erosion described above, an asset whose supply no government can expand is, in our view, the most direct answer to that risk. It is also among the most volatile assets an investor can own. It is scored like every other holding, but sized and handled under its own rules, and it is held whatever the thesis. Part 3 makes the full case and sets out the four valuation models that pace its buying: power-law bands, realized price, network adoption and production cost. A fifth reading, global liquidity, gives direction but sets no value.

Account placement matters most for strategies whose returns come from a few large wins. Over decades, where a convex holding sits (Roth, taxable, or pre-tax) can change the after-tax result by a wide margin; Parts 4 and 5 work the arithmetic and state their assumptions. At equal tax rates in and out, Roth and pre-tax end even. For convex, positions the balance tips toward Roth because the same dollar limit shelters more after-tax money in a Roth than in a pre-tax account, required distributions can push large pre-tax balances into higher brackets, and heirs generally inherit a Roth free of income tax under current law (Part 4).

For an investor building wealth for a family, the framework is a repeatable process; for an advisor, a documented alternative to fee-for-beta management, though not a substitute for a suitability process. Its case rests on a thesis that can be checked: the last section of this Part sets out the evidence that would prove it wrong.

Abstract

A portfolio operating system for unstable regimes.

The Adaptive Convexity Framework is built for unstable macro regimes: policy reflexivity, volatility clustering, skewed outcomes and shifting correlations. It anchors long-horizon conviction in Bitcoin. Positions are rated by the Convexity Integrity Score (), a weighted heuristic across four components (convexity and optionality, risk and fragility, macro alignment, and execution and sentiment), applied to each position at each weekly review and between reviews when a trigger fires. Part 6 sets out the method.

is used at several time scales in these pages. Unqualified in this Part, it means the structural regime: the conditions, read through growth, inflation and policy, that decide how assets behave for years at a time, and that a macro thesis describes (Part 2). Three shorter readings are named for their time scale: the cyclical weather (the growth-and-inflation map on the cover), the policy stance (read in the dashboard’s hawkish, dovish, stagflationary or neutral label) and the risk environment (risk-on, selective, transition or defensive). The dashboard reports the last two, as the box in the next section sets out.

Outside the Bitcoin backbone, every position carries a posture (Torque, Ballast or Hype), which lets the portfolio rotate across themes such as AI infrastructure, defense modernization, space commercialization, critical systems and biotechnology as the evolves.

placement follows what each holding is expected to do, held for good or rotated; Step 2 below gives the routing, and Part 4 works it through.

Risk is managed through predefined , set with each thesis: systemic stress indicators such as bond-market volatility (MOVE), liquidity conditions, breadth and credit spreads, and position-level signals such as CIS decay, momentum breakdown and valuation extension. Each is paired with a verification step (Step 7 below) to speed adaptation without inducing overtrading.

Borrowing against appreciated assets, through securities-backed lines of credit or Bitcoin-backed loans, can supply cash instead of a sale, and under current US law assets held until death generally pass to heirs with a stepped-up basis: the pattern. A loan adds interest cost and the risk of a forced, taxable sale if the collateral falls far enough or a payment is missed. Part 3 sets the rules for loans against Bitcoin: optional and late, inside conservative loan-to-value limits, and only to fund income-producing assets whose cash flow pays the interest, never living costs.

The method is designed to limit the cost of being wrong, catch thesis breaks early and redeploy capital by rule. The framework draws on Taleb’s fragility mathematics, Druckenmiller’s concentration discipline paired with active monitoring, Soros’s reflexivity dynamics, and Edelman’s longevity horizon work.

Order of Operations

The system at a glance.

  1. Macro thesis
  2. Wrapper placement
  3. Position sizing
  4. CIS band
  5. Momentum filter
  6. Tripwires
  7. Verification
  8. Adaptation
  9. Back to the thesis

The order matters because each stage feeds the next. Positions bought without a macro thesis are exposure with no reason behind them, and a thesis with no tripwires tends to break in silence, so the investor hears about it last.

  1. Macro thesis determines structure. If the operative thesis is the Fourth Turning (the crisis era in William Strauss and Neil Howe’s generational-cycle theory), structure tilts toward defense, critical infrastructure, parallel systems and hard assets. If it is a disinflationary technology boom (AI raising productivity, goods prices falling, asset prices rising), structure tilts toward AI infrastructure, semiconductors, cloud computing and technology platforms. Real theses often blend the two, as the example thesis in Part 2 does. A thesis makes no point forecast; it is a lens for spreading probability across regime scenarios. Whatever the thesis, Bitcoin is held as the backbone, sized and paced under the rules in Part 3.

  2. Structure determines wrapper placement. Torque that may rotate is directed to Roth accounts, where right-tail outcomes (which can reach 10 to 100 times the initial position) compound and rotate tax-free. Taxable accounts hold never-sold Bitcoin, return-of-capital Ballast, buy-and-hold positions beyond Roth capacity, and smaller satellite positions kept for tax-loss harvesting. Pre-tax accounts take the employer match, a deferral in an unusually high-income year, and ordinary-income payers such as bond funds where pre-tax space exists. On the match: contribute at least enough to earn the full employer match. Your own contribution can go into a Roth 401(k) bucket if the plan has one. The match itself is pre-tax unless the plan lets you elect Roth matching contributions, which SECURE 2.0 permits if the plan adopts it (the match must be fully vested and is taxable income in the year it is made). Part 4 sets out the full map.

  3. Wrapper placement decides what a size is worth. The size itself comes from the posture’s band table in Part 5, at the band the CIS selects in the next step, and concentration limits apply to the household total across every account. A Roth compounds the position without tax drag; in a taxable account, tax and the cost of realizing gains shrink the result.

  4. CIS selects the sizing band. For every holding except the Bitcoin backbone, posture sets the band table. The score selects the posture-specific sizing band: 70 or above supports core sizing, 60 to 69 standard sizing, 50 to 59 starter sizing, and below 50 is not allocation-worthy. The score is a structured judgment, uncertain by a few points either way; the bands absorb most of that uncertainty, though not at their edges. A material score change prompts a resizing review; at 50 and above, exits are governed by posture rules, tripwires and thesis evidence, not by the score band alone. Part 6 develops the full rubric and its weights. The step exists to stop “I like this stock” portfolio construction.

  5. CIS scores are confirmed by momentum. The reads the market’s vote on the thesis on three dimensions: distance from the 52-week high, strength relative to the sector and the market, and breadth. A position with CIS 75 and one broken momentum dimension has its sizing reduced 25 to 30 percent; with two broken it goes on watch with minimal new exposure; with all three broken (extended distance below the 52-week high, negative relative strength, declining breadth) it exits despite the score, per Part 5. CIS below 50 removes allocation eligibility at any momentum reading.

  6. Momentum is monitored by tripwires. Tripwires are written when the thesis is set, around the regime’s dominant fragilities. For the current thesis, the systemic set watches bond-market volatility (the MOVE index), equity volatility (the VIX), market breadth and widening credit spreads; at the position level, a sharp CIS decline and a momentum breakdown. A drawdown limit completes the set. Different theses produce different tripwire sets; a deflationary thesis, for example, might monitor M2 contraction and yield-curve dynamics instead. Part 5 sets the responses.

  7. Tripwires trigger verification. When a tripwire fires, the practitioner verifies it: is the signal noise (temporary volatility) or information (a thesis break)? can help with news flow, positioning data, sentiment indicators and historical analogs; human judgment makes the call.

  8. Verification informs adaptation. Verification sorts the response into one of four categories: watch (thesis intact, volatility normal), hedge (thesis weakening), trim (thesis breaking, reduce by 25 to 50 percent), or exit and redeploy (thesis broken, move the capital to higher-CIS opportunities). Deciding the categories in advance keeps a bad week from writing its own response.

  9. Adaptation feeds back into the macro thesis. When several positions in a theme breach CIS thresholds at the same time despite strong momentum, the thesis itself may be shifting. You refine the thesis as that evidence accumulates, or drop it if the evidence falsifies it (Part 2), and log each change, including each decision to change nothing.

Key Insight

This is a closed loop. Rules drive most decisions, recorded judgment drives the rest, and both leave a trail: every action should trace to a trigger and be logged.

Six failure modes recur, each with a named answer:

Narrative drift

Holding a deteriorating position because “I still believe in the story.” CIS forces a scored reassessment.

Recency bias

Overweighting recent winners or panic-selling recent losers. Momentum filters and tripwires set the rules before the panic arrives.

Fragility to correlation shifts

Assuming diversification holds under stress. A barbell structure and Ballast chosen for low factor correlation are meant to keep working when correlations jump.

Tax inefficiency

Putting holdings in whichever account had room, and losing terminal wealth to tax. Account placement is a design decision from the first dollar.

Attention scarcity

Missing thesis breaks under information overload. Tripwires watch the critical signals for you.

Emotional decision-making

Buying tops, selling bottoms, chasing performance. Written rules stand in for the impulse of the moment.

A governed process takes discretion away where it does damage (emotional sizing, holding on a narrative, ignoring tax) and leaves it where we think judgment can add value (thematic rotation, tactical positioning and adaptive use of borrowing).

The investor still makes every decision; the written rules mean the hardest ones were thought through on a calm day, before the selloff that tests them.

In the dashboard, as of September 2026

The dashboard computes CIS and the Framework Integrity Score (FIS, Part 6), watches the tripwires it has data for and displays each one’s prescribed response. It never executes a response. It records every trade and never blocks one, and it places no orders. It reports a macro label for the policy stance (hawkish, dovish, stagflationary or neutral, set by the direction of rates, inflation and unemployment; the dashboard and the Math page call it the macro regime) and a portfolio-level risk environment (risk-on, selective, transition or defensive). It does not yet measure the three momentum dimensions; Part 5 says what it watches instead. Its AI market briefing (Tape Read) reads the current tripwire states when it runs, and nothing launches research automatically when a tripwire fires. The Math page lists the thresholds the dashboard watches and marks which rules run in the software and which are written rules you carry out.

Survival comes first because only capital that survives can keep compounding.

Falsifiers

What would prove us wrong.

These are the tests we have set for the thesis of this Part. That thesis is our reading of the structural regime; the macro thesis that sets a portfolio’s structure belongs to the practitioner (Part 2), and the method does not change with either. Every test counts only from January 1, 2026: what happened before then is reported as history and does not count toward meeting a test. About nine months of that window had passed when we set them. Each test has public data, a window, a threshold set by our judgment with the history in view, and a stated consequence. A test that is not met is not evidence for us: most of these outcomes have causes other than the one we argue. The publication date, the release commit and an Internet Archive snapshot of this wording will be stamped here at release; if we ever change a test, we will say so and keep reporting against the original.

  1. The central bank stays in charge

    We would be wrong about fiscal dominance if, from January 2026, the Federal Reserve holds its policy rate at least a point above core PCE inflation for at least 24 consecutive months and, within that stretch, brings core PCE inflation to 2.5 percent or below, while federal interest costs are at least 3 percent of GDP. Through August 2026 the gap stayed below a point in every month; it was 0.6 points in August, before the September increase. The test does not count the 2023 to 2025 episode, but that episode is evidence against our reading: the gap held for 28 months, to November 2025, interest costs were at least 3 percent of GDP in fiscal 2024 and 2025, and core PCE inflation bottomed at 2.56 percent. At a 2.6 percent bar it would have met the test, and we set the 2.5 percent bar after that low was known. If it happens, we stop treating fiscal dominance as a constraint of this regime.

  2. Bondholders are not paying

    We would be wrong that bondholders will bear part of the cost of this debt if 10-year Treasuries return more than 1.5 percent a year after inflation from 2026 through 2035, about their average since 1928. In the last liquidation, 1946 to 1974, they lost about 1 percent a year. If it happens, we withdraw the claim that relying on government bonds for a real return is a bet against the precedent.

  3. The hedge returns

    We would be wrong about the stock-bond correlation if, from January 2026, the 24-month correlation of monthly returns on US stocks and 10-year Treasuries is below zero at 12 consecutive month-ends. It was negative for most of 2000 to 2021, positive from March 2022 to September 2025, and negative again since October 2025: through June 2026, the latest month with complete data, it was below zero at all six month-ends the test counts so far, so the test is not met yet. If it happens, the diversifier we call broken is working again, and we rewrite the correlation case in this Part.

  4. The old portfolio delivers

    We would be wrong about the playbook itself if a 60/40 mix of US stocks and 10-year Treasuries returns at least 4 percent a year after inflation, before fees and taxes, from 2026 through 2035. The bar sits between the mix’s 3.3 percent in the last liquidation and its 7.8 percent in the falling-rate decades, and below its 5.2 percent average since 1928. If it happens, we say so and rewrite this Part’s case. If it does not, that alone does not prove us right: high starting valuations can hold returns down in any regime.

The exact method, the data and the history behind each threshold are on the Evidence page, with the script that computes the readings. We will publish the readings each February, including the years when nothing changes. These tests check the thesis, not the framework: whether following the framework does better than a simple portfolio after costs and taxes is a separate question that nothing here answers yet. A single bad year proves nothing in either direction, and neither does a Bitcoin drawdown; Part 3 judges the backbone against ten requirements and lists what could break it.

Scope

These pages set out a written doctrine. It makes no point forecasts and guarantees no return; it does make directional claims about this regime, and the tests above say what would prove them wrong. The framework is a designed process, not a fitted model. Its rules and scores have not been backtested against a benchmark; where these pages describe outcomes, they describe what the design intends unless a figure is labeled as measured. Apart from Part 1’s sequence-of-returns exhibit, the worked examples in these Parts assume you are not yet drawing on the portfolio. The framework does not yet publish a withdrawal policy for a portfolio you live on. The method carries across account types and investor profiles; the tax material is written for US accounts, and tax and borrowing treatments are described under current US law as of September 2026 and can change. The audit trail is a design goal, not a legal standard. This framework does not constitute investment, tax, or legal advice.
